name: Meditation / mindfulness

lead: Meditation and mindfulness train attention and non-judgmental awareness of the body, thoughts and surroundings. People in appearance and self-improvement circles use them to lower stress and improve self-image, which they link to a calmer, steadier presence.

Practitioners focus attention on breath, body or thoughts without judgement. Reviews report benefits for stress, pain and mood in some populations, though a 2012 meta-analysis excluded almost three quarters of 595 identified studies for methodological problems. Stress effects are widely studied; no studies test appearance outcomes.

paras: People practise for short daily sessions, using guided audio, apps or classes, and combine it with sleep, exercise and other routines. Effects on stress and attention are usually described over weeks of regular practice.
The sources reviewed document no physical risks. Critics note commercialisation and inconsistent definitions of mindfulness.

angle.text: Appearance and self-improvement communities use meditation to lower stress and improve self-image, which they link to a calmer demeanour and more relaxed presence. Stress effects are widely studied; effects on appearance specifically are not.

lead: Meditation is a family of attention-training practices, and mindfulness, the form most often discussed today, is deliberate and usually nonjudgmental awareness of bodily sensations, feelings, thoughts and surroundings.[1] In appearance and self-improvement communities it is used mainly as a way to lower stress, steady mood and sharpen self-awareness, which proponents link to better sleep, more consistent training and skincare routines, calmer presentation and a kinder relationship with one's own image.

The practice has a long history in Buddhist, Hindu, Taoist and other contemplative traditions, and entered Western medicine in the 1970s: Herbert Benson's relaxation response in 1975 and Jon Kabat-Zinn's Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) at the University of Massachusetts in 1979.[1][2][3] Today it ranges from eight-week clinic programs to phone apps, and from secular stress management to Transcendental Meditation and Zen.[1][4][5]

Research is large but methodologically uneven. A 2014 JAMA Internal Medicine review of 47 trials reported moderate evidence that mindfulness programs reduce anxiety, depression and pain, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 58 studies found stress-management interventions, mindfulness and meditation included, lowered cortisol.[6][7] No studies have tested meditation for physical appearance outcomes.
infobox: Buddhist traditions (sati, vipassana, Zen), Hindu and other contemplative traditions
Eight weekly group sessions plus a day-long retreat and daily home practice
Focused attention, open monitoring, mantra (Transcendental Meditation), loving-kindness

paras: Meditation is often grouped into focused (concentrative) practices, such as attention on the breath, a mantra or loving-kindness, and open-monitoring practices, which cultivate non-reactive awareness of whatever arises, including mindfulness and Zen shikantaza.[4] Transcendental Meditation uses a silently repeated, individually assigned mantra for about 15 to 20 minutes twice a day.[5] Vipassana pairs insight with calm abiding, and Zen centres on seated zazen and walking meditation.[4] Researchers have also proposed grouping practices by activation level and body orientation instead of the focused/open split.[4]

The English word mindfulness was used by T. W. Rhys Davids in 1881 to render the Pali sati. Scholars debate whether the modern gloss of bare attention captures the older term, which also involves ethical discernment.[1] Practice often includes a body scan, in which attention moves through the body region by region, a method MBSR adapted from a Burmese vipassana tradition.[1][2]

Records of meditation appear in the Upanishads and the Yoga Sutras, in Taoist texts such as the Zhuangzi, and in Christian, Sufi and Buddhist traditions; Buddhist practice reached China in the 2nd century CE and Japan in the 6th.[4] Meditation spread in the West from the late 19th century, helped by D. T. Suzuki's writings on Zen, the Insight Meditation Society (founded 1976) and Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, who began teaching Transcendental Meditation publicly in India in 1955 and toured internationally from 1958; celebrity followers raised its profile in the 1960s and 1970s.[1][5]

Jon Kabat-Zinn, born in 1944 and trained as a molecular biologist at MIT, founded the Stress Reduction Clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in 1979 and renamed its eight-week course MBSR. He removed the explicit Buddhist framing to present the program within a scientific rather than religious frame.[2][3] His books include Full Catastrophe Living (1990 or 1991, depending on the source) and the bestselling Wherever You Go, There You Are (1994), and a 1993 PBS special on mind-body healing made him widely known.[2][3] Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy, developed by Segal, Williams and Teasdale, later adapted the approach to prevent depression relapse.[1] By 2015 nearly 80 percent of US medical schools offered some mindfulness training, and the COVID-19 pandemic pushed many practitioners toward phone apps.[1][2]

MBSR is an eight-week group course of roughly 2.5 to 3 hour weekly sessions with an all-day, often silent retreat between weeks six and seven; participants practise guided meditation, body scans and gentle yoga at home for about 45 to 60 minutes on six days a week.[2] Many people instead practise on their own for shorter periods, using apps, books or recordings. A 2019 randomized trial tested an eight-week mindfulness app (Calm) against a wait-list control in college students with elevated stress.[8]

In looksmaxxing and self-improvement forums, meditation appears in guides listing several styles (mindfulness, focused, and others), in recommendations alongside sleep and exercise, and in threads about binaural beats and visualisation.[9][10][11]

The 2014 JAMA Internal Medicine review screened 18,753 citations and included 47 randomized trials with 3,515 participants. It reported moderate evidence of reduced anxiety (effect size 0.38 at 8 weeks), depression (0.30) and pain (0.33) with mindfulness programs, low evidence for stress and quality of life, and low or insufficient evidence for sleep, eating habits and weight; meditation was not shown to be better than active treatments such as drugs, exercise or other behavioural therapies.[6]

A 2018 meta-analysis of 142 samples and 12,005 participants found mindfulness-based interventions outperformed no treatment (d = 0.55) and non-specific active controls (d = 0.35) at post-treatment, and did not differ from evidence-based treatments; the strongest support was for depression and pain.[12] A 2024 meta-analysis of 58 randomized studies (3,508 participants) found stress-management interventions lowered cortisol (g = 0.282), with mindfulness and meditation at g = 0.345.[7] A 2017 meta-analysis of 45 studies with active controls found meditation reduced markers including cortisol, blood pressure and heart rate depending on the style.[13]

A 2014 randomized trial examined mindfulness meditation for chronic insomnia.[14] A 2009 study found experienced meditators outperformed meditation-naive controls on measures of attentional performance and cognitive flexibility.[15] A 2015 trial of 75 volunteers reported that mindfulness meditation reduced pain through mechanisms different from placebo.[16] Reviews of neuroimaging describe changes in attention- and emotion-related regions, and a 2019 review discusses mindfulness and interoception, awareness of internal bodily signals.[17][18]

Reviews have examined MBSR, MBCT and Zen meditation for depression, anxiety, pain and distress,[19] stress-management programmes for medical students,[20] mindfulness in nurses,[21] and sitting meditation in youth.[22] A 2023 randomized trial compared three five-minute breathwork exercises with mindfulness meditation over a month for mood and arousal.[23] Wikipedia notes that a 2021 Cochrane review could not confirm MBSR's usefulness for medical students and junior doctors because of few studies and risk of bias.[2]

Controlled studies address stress, anxiety, depression, pain, attention, cortisol and sleep in clinical and general populations.[6][7][12][14] A 2007 evidence report and a 2012 meta-analysis noted methodological limits, the latter excluding almost three quarters of 595 identified studies for design problems.[24][25] No studies found that test meditation for appearance outcomes such as skin, weight or facial features.

Early research was criticised for weak methods and inconsistent definitions; newer work increasingly uses randomized trials with active controls.[1][4] Some scholars argue psychology narrows mindfulness to attention and drops its ethical components, and critics use the term McMindfulness for a commercialised, productivity-focused version.[1] Critics including Christopher Titmuss and Ronald Purser have also questioned the adaptation of MBSR for military use, which Kabat-Zinn reportedly approved.[3]

Wikipedia notes that a 2026 systematic review of mindfulness in children found few studies checked for harms.[2] Online discussion of reports that meditation can worsen depression or anxiety in some people has circulated, for example in a 2020 Hacker News thread.[26] Transcendental Meditation has been the subject of court decisions on whether it is religious and of scientific criticism of some of its claims.[5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, meditation is discussed in how-to guides, in debates over whether it is 'cope' and in threads on binaural beats and visualisation; posters frequently separate the research on mindfulness from mystical claims.[9][10][11]
